turei-zahav.1#_: Because it is noten taam bar noten taam of heter. Explanation: at first there is no substance of meat, only taste — that is, the meat imparted taste to the bowl and the bowl to the fish and still all is heter; and such a weak taste has no prohibition; but in a prohibition, even many times noten taam bar noten taam, all is forbidden.
turei-zahav.2#א: And even in the shell. The egg shell is clearly perforated, and when a person cooks it he finds the egg itself colored from that color; therefore the Sages forbade an egg of a chick and permitted a forbidden egg, for that one emits broth of a chick and this one emits only mere broth, end of his words Rashba, and Beit Yosef brings it; and requires study from what Rama wrote in siman 86 seif 5 that if the egg is pierced its law is like peeled, for every egg shell is perforated and it emits well; and even so it is permitted in a forbidden egg that emits only broth — why distinguish a hole that developed or did not develop; and if not for the holy mouth of Rashba, it appears to me there is no hole in an egg by nature, but rather it absorbs and emits through the shell from something that is actually in it — and requires study.
turei-zahav.2#ב: And there are those who are stringent with roasting and cooking. For in this it is like actual meat in fish, and they did not permit noten taam bar noten taam except when it came up by itself — that is, fish boiling immediately after they removed them from the fire and placed them in a cold meat bowl, or the reverse where the fish are cold and the bowl is boiling — it is permitted to eat them with milk; but when both are hot, the fish and the bowl are forbidden, for according to this it is like when they were cooked or roasted. And some say that here it appears specifically with milk the fish is forbidden, but by itself it is permitted — behold there is still a prohibition because of danger, as he wrote in siman 116 that there is danger if fish was cooked with meat; here we did not descend to that law except regarding noten taam bar noten taam; and so too Rashal in chapter 35 siman 76; but in Issur VeHeter general rule 39 he wrote and these are his words: and so any matter that is because of emission of vessels — they do not forbid from meat to fish b'dieved because of danger of something else, for they permit in the Gemara fish that came up in a boiling meat bowl — and requires study according to this from what I mentioned here. But what they said in this — fish that came up in a bowl, etc. — one may learn from this that there is no danger in eating fish that has taste of meat from what was cooked in a ben yomo meat vessel, for they said in the Gemara that many ate fish that came up in a bowl, etc.; and see siman 116 what he wrote there.
turei-zahav.2#ג: And the custom is to forbid l'chatchila. It appears that without cooking, but only came up by itself, it is permitted even l'chatchila; and so too Rama afterward explicitly; and this is like the words of Sefer HaTerumah that Beit Yosef brings — legumes cooked in a dairy pot are permitted l'chatchila to pour them into a ben yomo meat pot; and automatically for us, who are stringent in cooking, at least regarding came up it is permitted l'chatchila; except that Beit Yosef wrote that this disagrees with what Semak wrote — that l'chatchila it is forbidden to bring them up in a meat vessel in order to eat them afterward with kutach; and so I saw in Rashal chapter 25 siman 63, and he was not precise, for Semak also permits afterward l'chatchila with kutach, but l'chatchila he forbids bringing them up in a meat vessel for this reason, end of his words — therefore Rama is well lenient even without cooking even l'chatchila; but it is forbidden l'chatchila to bring them up in a meat vessel in order to eat afterward with kutach; and so too Issur VeHeter general rule 34 in name of Semag — that it is forbidden to cause noten taam bar noten taam l'chatchila even by bringing up without cooking; and in cooking it is forbidden l'chatchila even to pour afterward to milk. And Rashal wrote and these are his words: and since the world treats as forbidden when they were cooked, if so when they were cooked in a vessel that is not ben yomo it is also forbidden l'chatchila, for any taste for spoilage is forbidden l'chatchila — investigate; specifically the pot in which the food was cooked — they treat the food like the pot forever; but if a ben yomo meat spoon stuck into a pot that is not ben yomo, we permit to eat it with milk like the pot, for they were not stringent about sticking in the spoon which is accidental and a small amount, and the majority is that the spoon is clean, end of his words. In short, it appears from his language that also in a pot of milk it is forbidden to place the fish l'chatchila whenever it was first cooked in a meat vessel; and not like Rama who is lenient nearby even l'chatchila in their pots, also in a pot of meat that is not ben yomo Rama is lenient nearby; one who relies on Rama to be lenient in this has not lost.
turei-zahav.2#ד: But to place them like their vessels is permitted, etc. For in this we rely on those who permit also in cooking and roasting noten taam bar noten taam.
turei-zahav.2#ה: Against the meat absorbed. And if the absorbed amount is unknown, one needs sixty against all the spice.
turei-zahav.3#א: It is clear to me that there was no fat at all. One may not challenge from what Tosafot and Rosh and Ran that I brought in siman 97 seif 2 wrote — that they hold like Rabbeinu Tam who holds an oven is not cleaned well — one may say that there it deals with an oven that cannot be controlled so much by hand and requires great wiping needed for earthenware vessels, which is not so here in a bowl; and so too in a pot one controls it well with great wiping. And Maharach wrote: because of this Rosh here and Ran in chapter Kol HaBasar and in chapter Kli Sheni disagree with Rabbeinu Tam and hold it is cleaned well; and incidentally in his preoccupation with the text he did not look at Rosh and Ran chapter 25 who explicitly wrote like Rabbeinu Tam.
turei-zahav.3#ב: And there are those who forbid even if there is no fat, etc. Their reason is explained in Tosafot — for fish that came up in a bowl, this case is different here, since the bowls touch the pan and taste is emitted from one to the other and it becomes a second taste in prohibition; and further, when the second taste of meat and milk enters the water they are immediately forbidden and return and forbid the bowls and the pan, end of his words. And in Ran the second reason of Tosafot is explained further — this case is different in fish that came up in a bowl, etc., for kutach did not receive taste at all from the first taste, that is the bowl, but from the fish which is a second taste; but here the taste of milk that fell into the water receives taste from the first taste of meat in the bowls — for who will tell us that emission of meat and emission of milk will not mix in themselves without the intermediary of the water, end of his words. And nevertheless, if water or vegetables were cooked in a dairy ben yomo pot and one stuck into it a ben yomo meat spoon and there is not sixty against the ben yomo spoon, they forbid one another even if both were well scraped; and even though this is the actual law of bowls that were rinsed in a cauldron that Shulchan Aruch mentioned, nevertheless I wrote this because it is most common.
turei-zahav.3#ג: And then all the vessels are permitted. The one that is ben yomo is permitted, for it receives spoilage; and the one that is not ben yomo is also not forbidden from the one that is ben yomo, for it is noten taam bar noten taam and it is still heter even after it entered this vessel, since it is not ben yomo automatically there is no prohibition on it, end of his words — permitted even for the first reason of Tosafot above that they touch the pan, etc.; and according to what Rama wrote in siman 94 seif 5 to forbid the vessel that is not ben yomo as a stringency, he should have written here too, for it is one reason; and it appears that specifically there he holds one should be stringent because of marit ayin, since one pours food into a vessel that is as if it were ben yomo — therefore one forbids the vessel that is not ben yomo, and this does not apply here; so it appears to me to be Rama's intent.
turei-zahav.3#ד: And the water — they treat it with prohibition. For it absorbed now from spoiled meat and milk, and b'dieved does not apply in mere water as in a dish and pot which are significant items, and the Torah had pity on the money of Israel — Issur VeHeter general rule 34.
turei-zahav.3#ה: But if they were rinsed one after the other. Even in a kli rishon, for this is noten taam bar noten taam since the tastes did not mix.
turei-zahav.3#ו: Or in a kli sheni, etc. — all is permitted. Explanation: even if they were soiled, as he wrote afterward regarding pouring; and all the more so, for pouring is stricter than kli sheni for us. And Maharshal in chapter Kol HaBasar siman 64 disagrees on this and wrote that if there was grime from meat and milk it forbids even in a kli sheni, for there is concern the grime will dissolve in the water and be considered as the substance of the prohibition; however since this is somewhat a stringency, the teacher need not ask about this if they were soiled until it becomes clear to him automatically that they were soiled; but regarding pouring, which absorbs and emits up to kedei kelipah, food remnants are certainly forbidden, and one must ask if the rinsing was by way of pouring, since stam they are accustomed to pour on them from a kli rishon by the fire — if it is not known that it was not by pouring, then one need not ask if there was food remnant, end of his words. And it appears to me for practical halachah to decide that regarding pouring one must forbid both if there was food remnant from both; and if one is soiled and the second clean, then the clean becomes forbidden; but in a kli sheni food remnants do not forbid, since we establish that in a kli sheni even yad soledes bo does not absorb and does not emit, as Turei Chayim wrote general rule 57. It is written in Issur VeHeter that there is no difference if one rinsed in a kli rishon bowls with bowls or what they call in foreign tongue ladles — we do not say that what is used in a kli sheni does not forbid; since they place hot meat on it by way of pouring, if so through many pourings the prohibition is absorbed in all of it; kli sheni — the spoons that are accustomed to stick in a kli rishon; but if it is certain he did not use a kli rishon within twenty-four hours, it does not forbid b'dieved. And Maharach wrote: he agreed with Issur VeHeter.
turei-zahav.3#ז: Its law is like a kli rishon. One may challenge — behold it is noten taam bar noten taam; and it appears that since we forbid above as those who forbid whom Rama brought in this seif, because it is like taste of meat and milk mixed together — that is, since the two tastes mix in one vessel and chein nafsho — it is comparable to our considering the splash of pouring as if it were in the vessel from which he pours; therefore he forbids the vessel onto which he pours since it too is ben yomo; but if this vessel onto which he pours is not ben yomo, it is not forbidden, for it is no worse than that which he wrote nearby that the vessels are permitted if one is not ben yomo; so it appears to me.
turei-zahav.3#ח: We are not concerned lest they were rinsed in it. In Issur VeHeter it is written: even if they are accustomed in that house to rinse in a kli rishon they are permitted through a double doubt — a doubt lest they were not rinsed with them, and if you say they were rinsed, a doubt lest it was not ben yomo.
turei-zahav.4#_: For through ash it is noten taam lefegem. And according to this there is no prohibition if lye called zeif made from milk fell into a dish, for the lye has ash when they make it from milk, and requires study regarding this ruling, for above in siman 87 Rama wrote that the vessel in which they make water for head-washing, etc., and it is customary to mix meat and milk there, end of his words; and since noten taam lefegem, there is no basar b'chalav prohibition at all. And I also found in Rashal's words chapter 25 siman 94 and these are his words: and I found in name of Maharil that once a child came and said a piece of lye made from milk fell into the pot, and he said one should not believe the child, end of his words — it appears that if it certainly fell, the lye forbids; and behold lye is made from ash with milk and is noten taam lefegem, and requires study for practical halachah.
turei-zahav.5#_: One does not place, etc. The taste in salt: kutach that falls on it is visible and is not nullified, and we are concerned lest one salt meat in it; but in vinegar the prohibition is not visible and it is nullified in sixty.
turei-zahav.6#_: Permitted to place inside a chest, etc. For with meat and milk people are careful that nothing falls from one to the other.
turei-zahav.7#_: And one who is stringent also in this — blessing shall come upon him. This he wrote following Tosafot and Rosh chapter Kol HaBasar and these are his words: one may learn from here that pure salted and impure unsalted do not require hagalah — cheese molds of gentiles, etc.; and the wood does not become hot through salting; and they act every day that salt placed in a bowl used for meat — they take from it to place into milk and are not concerned lest it absorbed from the bowl; and one who is stringent — blessing shall come upon him, end of his words. The Rav understood that what Tosafot concluded "and one who is stringent — blessing" also refers to what he wrote "and they act every day," etc.; and this is very astonishing — for if he wrote "and they act every day," etc., he brings important learned men — are they among those who exclude themselves from blessing? Rather it is clear that "one who is stringent — blessing" refers to cheese molds of gentiles where we find stringencies in some poskim; but regarding this salt there is no reason to forbid even l'chatchila; and what Tosafot wrote "and they act every day" they wrote only as proof for the previous matter. And I also found afterward in Rashal chapter 25 siman 81 that the law of salt is permitted even l'chatchila; and he brought in Turei Chayim from Orach Chaim that clean gentile vessels — it is permitted to place there spices and other sharp things that do not emit a hard thing when dry, end of his words — I brought it in siman 91 seif 2; and Rashal concluded: and nevertheless I praise the Ashkenaz custom of having vessels made for salt, one for meat and one for milk, for sometimes during the meal one's hands are soiled from meat and he takes salt there and afterward will take for milk, and likewise the reverse, end of his words.
